title: Raw Concrete Interiors: A Lesson for California Luxury Homes
subtitle: A 1970s Belgian villa makes the case that raw concrete is a finish to be designed, not a structure to be hidden.
meta_description: Can raw concrete interiors feel warm? A 1970s Belgian villa pairs béton brut with leather and velvet — a design lesson for California luxury homes.
meta_keywords: raw concrete interiors, béton brut, concrete home California, reinforced concrete villa, luxury concrete architecture, Italian villa California, fair-faced concrete, concrete design Los Angeles
quick_answer: A 1970s Belgian villa profiled by AD Middle East shows raw concrete need not read as cold: béton brut walls are warmed by leather, velvet and smoked glass, and a sculptural outdoor shower is cast in situ as a single object. The lesson — concrete is a finish to design, not just a structure to hide.

faq.q: Is raw concrete a good material for luxury home interiors?
faq.a: Yes, when it is treated as a finish rather than a leftover structural surface. The Belgian villa profiled by AD Middle East pairs béton brut with leather, velvet and smoked glass — soft materials that borrow concrete's weight while removing any sense of chill. Specified for tone and texture, concrete reads as warm and tactile.

Béton brut — French for 'raw concrete' — is concrete left exposed with the imprint of its formwork, rather than clad or plastered over. It became a signature of mid-century architecture and, as the 1970s Belgian villa shows, works as a deliberate interior finish when paired with warmer materials and good light.

our_perspective: We read a villa like this as vindication of a simple conviction: concrete is a finishing material, not merely a structural one. The warmth people claim to miss in concrete comes entirely from how it is cast, toned and paired — which is why our villas are built in architectural concrete by DGU, the firm behind Renzo Piano's Kimbell Art Museum and Tadao Ando's Palazzo Grassi. We offer five facade tones and fair-faced surfaces precisely because béton brut rewards attention. Set it against wood, linen and stone, and the material built to endure also becomes the one you most want to touch.
body_html:
AD Middle East has profiled a 1970s Belgian villa that treats raw concrete as the entire vocabulary of a home — structure, surface and sculpture at once. The house sets béton brut walls against leather, velvet and smoked glass, and its most photographed gesture is a sculptural outdoor shower cast in situ: concrete poured in place and left to read as a single continuous object. Four decades on, it is a reminder that concrete was once the most expressive material in domestic architecture — and that, for the people who built with it, its warmth was never in doubt.

Why doesn't this concrete villa feel cold?

Because the concrete here is a backdrop for touch, not an end in itself. According to AD Middle East, the villa sets béton brut against leather, velvet and smoked glass — soft, light-absorbing materials that borrow the concrete's gravity while cancelling any chill. The cast-in-situ shower proves the logic in reverse: left bare and shaped with care, concrete stops being a wall and becomes sculpture.

A 1970s house, a raw-concrete shell, and three deliberate material pairings — the whole case for concrete as a finish, made in one villa.

How the Belgian villa pairs raw concrete (Source: AD Middle East)
ElementMaterial pairingEffect
Primary wallsBéton brut + leatherWarmth and grain against mass
UpholsteryVelvetAbsorbs and softens light
GlazingSmoked glassDims and filters the interior
Outdoor showerCast-in-situ concreteReads as a single sculptural object

What the villa documents is a discipline that much contemporary luxury construction has lost: concrete specified for how it would look and feel, not merely for how it would carry load. The formwork is part of the design. The tone is part of the design. The adjacency to a hide, a weave, a pane of grey glass is part of the design.

What can California luxury homes learn from béton brut?

That concrete belongs in the room, not hidden behind it. In a market where fire-exposed Los Angeles neighbourhoods are quietly shifting toward non-combustible structure, the easy mistake is to treat concrete as an engineering concession — poured, then plastered and clad until it disappears. The Belgian villa argues the opposite, and it argues it on purely aesthetic grounds.

For a Westside or Malibu commission, the implications are concrete in both senses. A reinforced-concrete envelope can be left fair-faced, toned warm, and set against the Mediterranean palette California already loves — olive wood, limewash, woven textiles, stone. Owners spend fortunes cladding resilient structures in combustible finishes to soften them; the smarter move is to design the concrete to be the finish. The 1970s got there first, with leather and velvet and a shower you would want to stand in.

  • Specify concrete tone and formwork texture as finish decisions, not afterthoughts.
  • Pair raw surfaces with warm, light-absorbing materials — leather, velvet, timber, linen.
  • Use smoked or tinted glazing to control interior light against the concrete's grey.

Concrete has spent fifty years being mischaracterised as the cold option. A single Belgian house, leather-lined and cast with intent, is enough to retire the cliché — and to suggest that the most durable surface in the home can also be its most sensual. The question for California's next generation of villas is not whether to build in concrete, but whether to have the nerve to leave it showing.
